In the last video, you saw how production can reveal situations
that never made it into your offline benchmark.

Now, let's follow one of those situations all the way through the
improvement loop with Northwind. First, look at the offline results.

Suppose Northwind has a policy compliance score of 96%.
That sounds pretty good, and it may be.

But before you conclude that the agent handles refunds reliably,
it's worth looking at the cases that produced that score.
Most of the refund examples in the test set are very direct.

A customer says, "Refund order 1842," or, "I want a refund for order
2271." Those are useful cases.

They show that when the customer states the intent clearly,
the agent can recognize the request and follow the refund process.

But then, a real customer writes, "I bought this last week
and it doesn't fit. Can I get my money back?"

They never used the word "refund", but that's clearly
what they're asking for.

So you search the offline dataset for similar examples
and you don't find one.

The test set contains explicit refund requests,
but nothing phrased this way. That's an important distinction.

It doesn't mean the 96% score was wrong.
The score told you how the agent performed on the cases you gave it.

Production has now shown you a case the tests didn't cover.
So let's open the trace and see what happened.
The customer says the item doesn't fit and asks for their money back.

Instead of recognizing that as a refund request,
the agent responds more like this is a general product complaint:
"I'm sorry it didn't work out.

Would you like to fill out our feedback form?"
That's a sympathetic answer, but it never enters the refund process.

And you can see that in the trajectory. There's no customer
verification, no order lookup, and no refund tool call.
So the problem starts before any of those tools come into play.

The agent never recognized that this message should trigger
the refund workflow.

Now you have something much more useful than a failed production
conversation. You have a concrete behavior you can reproduce and test.

Take the customer's original message and add it to your offline
dataset exactly as it appeared:
"I bought this last week and it doesn't fit.
Can I get my money back?"

Keeping the original phrasing matters because that phrasing is part of
what your existing benchmark was missing.
Then write down what the agent should do in this case.

It should recognize that the customer wants a refund,
follow the refund policy,

and perform whatever customer and order checks are required
before processing it.

You can then use the evaluators you already have to check those
parts of the behavior.

A policy evaluator can tell you whether the refund
rules were followed,

and your tool evaluators can check whether the required lookups
and actions actually happened.

At this point, something important has changed. This is no longer a
production failure that you happened to observe once.

It's now a test case you can run every time you modify the agent.
The trace also gives you a clue about where to look next.

The failure happens before the agent calls any refund tools, because
it never recognizes the request as a refund in the first place.

So one place worth investigating is the instruction that tells the
agent when to enter the refund workflow.
You might also look at the examples the agent has been given.

If every refund example says something explicit like
"refund this order",

the agent may not have enough guidance for requests such
as "can I get my money back?"

That gives you a direction for your next change,
You could clarify the refund routing instruction,

or maybe add a few examples that express refund
intent in different ways.
The exact change depends on how the Northwind agent is implemented.

So you wouldn't want to guess the final fix from this trace alone,
but now you have a concrete hypothesis to test.

And when you test it, don't run only the new production case.
run the older refund examples, too.

You still want refund order 1842 to work exactly as it did before.
Then run the rest of your known-good cases as well.
If you make the agent more sensitive to indirect refund requests,

you want to make sure it doesn't start interpreting ordinary product
questions as refunds.
So your benchmark has gotten bigger.

It still contains the refund cases you already knew about
and the other behaviors you've been protecting.
And now it also contains this new production case.

That means you should run the updated agent on that expanded benchmark
with the same evaluators.

Then look first at the case that came from production.
When the customer says, "I bought this last week and it doesn't fit.

Can I get my money back?", does the agent now recognize the refund
intent and enter the right workflow?

If it does, check the other refund cases next. Do those still work?
And then look at the rest of the benchmark.

Did anything else change that you didn't intend? This is the same
improvement process you've been using throughout the module.

The only difference is where this particular test case came from.
It came from a real customer.

And if you fix the behavior, you keep the case.
You don't remove it because the problem is gone.

That customer has shown you one way that the agent can
fail, and from now on,

future versions should have to prove that they don't
bring the failure back.

That's how your benchmark gets stronger over time.
Some cases begin as failures you discover during development.

Others begin as capabilities you want the agent to gain.
Others come from regressions introduced by your own changes.

And yet others come from production, because real users will always
create situations you didn't think to write down in advance.

Each time that happens, you can take what you learned and add it to
the next evaluation.

By the time you've gone through several rounds of improvement, you're
no longer testing the agent against the benchmark you started with.

You're testing it against a record of what you've
learned about the system.

the failures that mattered, the behaviors you fixed,
and the cases you now know you need to protect.

And that's the improvement stage of the process.
You started this module with the evaluation results already in hand.

You had traces, datasets, and evaluators that could show you where the
agent was succeeding and where it was failing.

Then, you use that evidence to choose what to improve, make a targeted
change, and compare the new version against the old one.

And as you saw, improving your agent is rarely about one
change and one result.

A fix can solve the problem you were aiming at and still introduce a
regression somewhere else.

So, you inspect what changed, look at the traces,
refine the intervention, and run the comparison again.

Once the agent is in production, real users give you new cases to
bring back into that same loop.

And that brings us to the end of this course. So let's zoom back out
to the full evaluation framework you've been working through.
The first stage in the process was to Observe.

You looked closely at what the agent actually did,
found failures in its responses and actions,
and gathered the evidence that showed where things went wrong.
Then came Benchmark.

You took those individual failures and turned them into criteria you
could apply consistently across many different cases.

You worked out what should count as a pass, what should count
as a failure, and created examples with the judgments you expected.

In Evaluate, you turn those criteria into automated checks
and tested how well those checks agreed with human judgment.

Once you trusted the evaluation setup, you could use it to measure the
agent across a larger set of cases.

And finally, in Improve, you use those measurements
to improve the system.

You found the patterns that mattered, chose where to intervene,
tested changes against the stable benchmark,

checked for regressions and trade-offs, and kept adding new evidence
as the agent encountered the real world.

And then, the cycle continues. Improve gives you new traces to
investigate. New failures may lead you to refine your criteria.

New behavior may require you to update your evaluations, and those
evaluations then give you the evidence for the next improvement.

So the four stages connect into one ongoing process: Observe,
Benchmark, Evaluate, Improve.
The goal isn't just to know whether an agent is good or bad.

It's to build a process that helps you understand the behavior of your
agent, measure it in a way you can trust,
and make better decisions about how to improve it.

That's the core of the evaluation loop, and that brings us to the end
of this course. Congratulations!

I hope you find the skills you've learned here useful as you build AI
applications going forward.
